pointers.sentence: It holds a **matcher** as its `pattern`, and asks the matcher (`django/urls/resolvers.py:URLPattern`).
The expression begins with `^`, and for a pattern it ends with `\Z` (`django/urls/resolvers.py:_route_to_regex`).

The matcher keeps the dictionary of converters the cache returns, not a copy of it, so matchers made from one route for the same kind of entry while its expansion is cached share one dictionary between them, and what `URLResolver._populate` writes into it in place, for a namespaced include under a plain one, reaches them all ([Namespaces](namespaces.md#get_ns_resolver-a-resolver-made-for-the-namespace)) (`django/urls/resolvers.py:RoutePattern.__init__`, `django/urls/resolvers.py:_route_to_regex`, `django/urls/resolvers.py:URLResolver._populate`).

Only one with converters is matched with its expression, which, since it begins with `^`, can match only from the start of the text (`django/urls/resolvers.py:RoutePattern.match`).
**Why.** "Only use regex overhead if there are converters," says the comment above that test (`django/urls/resolvers.py:RoutePattern.match`).
Five are registered to begin with (`django/urls/converters.py:DEFAULT_CONVERTERS`).

Since a route is expanded as its call of `path` runs, a converter has to be registered before the call of `path` for any route that uses it, as the museum's URLconf does above its patterns (`django/urls/converters.py:register_converter`).

A converter is written as a class, but Django uses a single instance of it: the one `register_converter` made, or for a default the one its module made as it was imported (`django/urls/converters.py:DEFAULT_CONVERTERS`).

`_route_to_regex` puts that instance into the converters of every route that names it, so it serves every route, in every thread, for the life of the process (`django/urls/converters.py:get_converters`).

A pattern's expression that ends in `$` is matched with `re.Pattern.fullmatch`, which requires the whole text and, unlike `$` alone, does not let a trailing newline pass; every other expression, a resolver's or a pattern's without the `$`, with `re.Pattern.search`, under which nothing but its own anchors holds it to the start of the text or to its end (`django/urls/resolvers.py:RegexPattern.match`).

On both classes the attribute `regex` is a descriptor, an object on the class that is run when the attribute is read (`django/urls/resolvers.py:LocaleRegexRouteDescriptor`, `django/urls/resolvers.py:LocaleRegexDescriptor`).

`re_path` keeps the expression as text, and one that is not valid raises `ImproperlyConfigured`, with the compiler's reason, only when its matcher is asked for `regex`: by `RegexPattern.match` as a path reaches it, or by `URLResolver._populate` as the tables for reversing are built (`django/urls/resolvers.py:LocaleRegexDescriptor._compile`).
The import passes it, and so do the URL checks, which read its text and never compile it ([The URL checks, and listing the patterns](checks.md)) (`django/urls/resolvers.py:RegexPattern.check`).

Then every path that reaches its entry raises, one meant for an entry after it as much as one meant for it, and so does every `reverse` with the URLconf, whatever the name, since the tables are built from every entry's expression (`django/urls/resolvers.py:URLResolver._populate`).
The descriptor stores nothing when the compile fails, so each raises again, every time (`django/urls/resolvers.py:LocaleRegexDescriptor`).

Building the tables for reversing reads the expression of every entry's matcher, and after the first `reverse` with the museum's URLconf every one of them is compiled (`django/urls/resolvers.py:URLResolver._populate`).
